description: Our team is focused on using art and graphic design to create better mapping technology.
summary: What we're developing is an app intended for the NASA kids page and as a tool for educators. It can show the landing sites that are monitored by NASA data sources by their Horizons, their relative position on a 3-D representation of the moon, descriptions from characters on why you should choose one site versus another and, a calendar to show where there is solar activity on the various land positions based on any day of the year you choose. The challenge describes creation of a tool to identify solar energy to power stations on the moon in a way that is accessible to educators and students. Our app's simple UI and cute characters explain the science behind where to put new landing stations in a way that is engaging and fun for kids and educators. It's extremely important for NASA to be able to communicate with kids and educators because their projects are often very technical and hard to understand. This app allows kids to understand space exploration at organizations like NASA behind the scenes.
details:
Our project, the Southlight Lunar Landing Platform, is an interactive educational tool for exploring potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. Users can compare sunlight and Earth visibility at six candidate sites, inspect NASA lunar elevation data in maps and rotatable 3D views, and adjust a simple flight-status dashboard for fuel, altitude, and descent speed. The site comparison uses date-specific Sun and Earth positions from NASA’s JPL Horizons service, while the terrain views use elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA).

The project helps make lunar exploration easier to understand by letting users explore the data themselves. They can see how a site’s location may affect its view of the Sun and Earth, compare real terrain features, and consider how solar-panel size might affect an illustrative energy estimate. The intended impact is to support STEM learning and spark interest in space exploration by showing some of the real choices involved in planning a lunar mission.

We built the app in Python using Streamlit for the interface and Plotly for interactive charts and 3D graphics. We also used NumPy, Rasterio, and Requests to process terrain data and retrieve information from NASA services. Docker and Poetry help run and manage the software. It is designed to run on a standard computer in a web browser; no specialized hardware is required.

The project is creative because it combines scientific datasets with a hands-on mission-planning activity and friendly explanations from Nikko, a cartoon hippo guide drawn on iPad with Procreate . We considered how to make the experience engaging and understandable while keeping the data and its limits clear. For example, terrain is reduced to a manageable preview for display, and the Sun and Earth visibility estimates use a flat horizon, so they do not account for local ridges or crater shadows. The solar-panel energy estimate is also simplified, so the app is intended for learning and exploration rather than real mission planning.
